# Volcanic Stack: System Context for AI Agents (llms.txt)

> **AI AGENT DIRECTIVE**: this is the system context for `@volcanicminds/backend` **v5**. Read
> it before proposing architecture changes, generating services or debugging. **In any conflict,
> the package source code wins** — and where a section still shows a v4 shape, `README.md` and
> `docs/MIGRATION_V4_V5.md` win over this file.
>
> **Coming from 4.x?** `docs/MIGRATION_V4_V5.md` lists every break with the new form beside the
> old one. The short version of what is GONE and must never be generated:
>
> | Removed | Now |
> |---|---|
> | `@volcanicminds/backend/typeorm` | `@volcanicminds/backend/db` — the subpath names no engine |
> | TypeORM entities, `@Entity`, `@Column`, `BaseEntity` | Drizzle tables, built **per container** |
> | `req.db`, `req.runner` | `req.control`, `req.tenant` — two distinct types |
> | `global.connection`, `global.entity`, `global.repository` | nothing. There is no ambient container |
> | `executeFindQuery`, `executeCountQuery`, `applyQuery` | `executeFind`, `executeCount`, `parseQuery` |
> | `switchContext`, `runInTenantContext` | a job declares its plane and is handed a handle |
> | `options.multi_tenant` | the `control` and `tenants` blocks |
> | `page`, `pageSize`, `sort=f:desc` | `_page`, `_pageSize`, `_sort=-f` |
> | `:raw`, `:eqs`, `:isEmpty`, `:notNull` | removed. `:eq`, `:empty=true`, `:null=false` |
> | `DB_SYNCHRONIZE_SCHEMA_AT_STARTUP`, `POST /tool/synchronize-schemas` | committed migrations |
> | MongoDB, PGlite as a deployment engine | Postgres, SQLite, libSQL |

> **Core Paradigms (MANDATORY)**:
> 1. **Framework**: Node.js (v24+ required), Fastify v5, pure ESM (`NodeNext`).
> 2. **Architecture**: Thin Controllers, Fat Services. Controllers only map HTTP to Services. Services handle business logic and never know about HTTP.
> 3. **Data Layer**: `@volcanicminds/backend/db`, Drizzle underneath and that is an implementation detail. Reach data through a Service Layer bound to the request's **container** (`service.on(dataContext(req))`, importing `dataContext` from `@volcanicminds/backend`). There is no global connection to fall back on, and a call with no handle **throws** rather than guessing. Use Magic Query (`req.data()`) for filtering.
> 4. **Security**: row-level security goes in `applyPermissions` and travels as `QueryOptions.extraWhere`, which is AND-ed **after** everything the URL asked for — `_logic` included — so no filter a caller writes reaches around it. Do not bypass it.
> 5. **Failures are visible**: v5 has no silent fallbacks. A query with no container throws; an audit write that fails fails the request; a filter the engine cannot honour answers 400. Never "recover" by widening a scope.
> 6. **TypeScript**: strict typing required. Use the provided types (`FastifyRequest`, `FastifyReply`, `ControlHandle`, `TenantHandle`, `DataHandle`).

## How to read this document (3 audiences)

This file is the **single, self-contained source of truth** for `@volcanicminds/backend` **v5**. It is written so
that three different readers can use it without any other source:

1. **A developer new to the project** — wants to start a server, expose public and private
   routes, choose an auth mode, optionally add a database, optionally add `@volcanicminds/tools`, in single- or
   multi-tenant mode. → Start at **Part 0 (Mental Model)**, then **Part 12 (Usage Scenarios & Recipes)**.
2. **An LLM coding agent reading the repository directly** — needs exact, code-accurate API surface, types, and
   contracts to generate or modify code. → Treat **Part 10 (Manager contract)**, **Part 11 (Native API surface)**
   and the package source in `lib/` as authoritative; this doc summarizes them, the source wins on conflict.
3. **An LLM using only the Context7 MCP tool** (no repo access) — receives chunks of this file. Each Part is
   self-describing and cross-links the others, so a single retrieved Part is still actionable.

A fourth reader worth naming: **a working example**. `volcanic-backend-sample` is this document as a running
project, ported to v5 and verified against a real Postgres. Where the two disagree, the sample is the one that
runs.

## Part 0 — Mental Model (Core vs Data Layer)

`@volcanicminds/backend` ships **two cleanly separated layers** in one npm package:

- **The HTTP Core** (`@volcanicminds/backend`) — Fastify wrapper: routing autodiscovery, JSON-Schema validation,
  hooks, JWT/cookie auth, RBAC, MFA gatekeeper, Swagger, scheduler, and the **native API** (`/auth`, `/users`,
  `/token`, `/tenants`, `/system/*`, `/health`). **The core needs no database to run.** With no managers injected
  it boots on **Null-Object defaults** (every manager reports `isImplemented() === false`) — perfect for a pure
  public API.
- **The Data Layer** (subpath `@volcanicminds/backend/db`) — Magic Query, the framework's own tables, per-tenant
  containers, versioned migrations, and the concrete **managers** you inject into the core. Drizzle is what is
  behind it and is nobody's business: in v4 the subpath was `/typeorm`, so the ORM was part of the public API and
  replacing it broke every consumer. Its deps (`drizzle-orm`, `pg` or `better-sqlite3`/`@libsql/client`, `bcrypt`)
  are **optional peer dependencies**.

The two layers meet at exactly **one seam**: the data layer's `start()` returns the managers, and you hand those
to the core's `start(decorators)`. They are values you own, not singletons imported from a subpath, which is what
makes a different implementation a parameter rather than a patch.

The separation is **checked in CI** by `dependency-cruiser`: the core may not import `lib/database/**` or any of
its peer dependencies, and the data layer may import only *types* from the core. A rule a build enforces is a
rule; one a document states is a hope. (It is also why `uuid` and the environment reader exist twice — see
`lib/database/uuid.ts` and `lib/database/env.ts`.)

```
┌─────────────────────────── @volcanicminds/backend ───────────────────────────┐
│  HTTP CORE  (always present, DB-agnostic)                                     │
│    Fastify · routes · auth (Bearer/Cookie) · RBAC · MFA · native API · jobs   │
│                              ▲  start(decorators)                             │
│                              │  the managers the data layer returned          │
│  DATA LAYER  (optional, subpath /db, optional peer deps)                       │
│    Magic Query · framework tables · containers · migrations · managers        │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**The one thing to internalise before generating any data code**: a request is **handed** its
container and never reaches for one.

| | |
|---|---|
| `req.control` | the control plane: tenant registry, platform identities |
| `req.tenant` | this request's tenant container. Absent on a single-tenant deployment |
| `req.tenantInfo` | the registry row of that tenant. A record, never a connection |

`const container = dataContext(req)` is the whole idiom, and there is no third answer. Do not
write it out as `req.tenant ?? req.control`: that form hands a tenant route that lost its
container the control plane, instead of the error the framework raises.
In v4 this was `req.db`, an `EntityManager` a service could do without: a call with no context
fell back to `global.connection`, which meant reading whichever container the pool happened to
hold. That is defect D-01, and it was not theoretical — a tenant's `search_path` survived in the
pool, so a control-plane route could list another customer's users. In v5 there is no global to
fall back to and a manager called with nothing **throws**.

To reach inside a handle — for your own tables, or a query an ORM has no business expressing:

```ts
import { access } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'
const { db, dialect, locator, execute, transaction } = access(container)
```

`locator` is the load-bearing field: it is the schema (or file) this handle addresses, and what
your own table objects must be built for.

**Decision shortcuts:**
- *No persistence?* Use the core alone, expose public routes, inject nothing. (Part 12, Scenario A)
- *Need users/login/persistence?* Add the `/db` subpath, `await preload()`, then `startDataLayer()`, then hand the result to `startServer()`. (Scenarios C–F)
- *Need MFA / file upload / mail?* Add `@volcanicminds/tools` and inject `mfaManager` / `transferManager`. (Part 12.7)
- *Need tenant isolation?* **Declare the `tenants` block** — declaring it is what enables tenancy; there is no `enabled` flag to contradict the strategy. (Part 12.6)

### 6.1.1 Dual Mode Configuration

The system supports two mutually exclusive authentication modes, configurable via the `AUTH_MODE` environment variable.

1.  **Bearer Token Mode** (`AUTH_MODE=BEARER`): Standard behavior. Token is returned in login body and must be sent in `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. Ideal for Mobile Apps and S2S.
2.  **Cookie Mode** (`AUTH_MODE=COOKIE`): Browser-secure behavior. Token is set in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie. Login body does not contain the token. Client does not need to manage the token manually. Requires `COOKIE_SECRET` in `.env`.
    - **Logout**: In Cookie mode, the `/auth/logout` route clears the `auth_token` cookie.

    - **6.2 Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)**
      - Policy and "Gatekeeper" Flow (Pre-Auth Token)
      - Adapters and Tools
    - **6.3 Role Based Access Control (RBAC)**
      - Role Definition and Route Gatekeepers
    - **6.4 Context Injection & TypeScript**
      - Type extension and `preHandler` Hook
    - **6.5 Emergency Admin Reset**

# Part 1: Foundations and Infrastructure

This section covers the essentials for understanding how the framework orchestrates the server, the database, and global dependencies. It is not just about starting a Node.js process, but setting up a scalable, secure, and strongly-typed architecture.

## 1.1 Introduction and Stack Philosophy

The framework is an **opinionated** system composed of three modular packages working in synergy to eliminate _boilerplate code_.

### The Three Pillars

1.  **`@volcanicminds/backend` (Server Core)**
    - **Fastify** wrapper.
    - Manages the HTTP lifecycle, automatic route loading (`Auto-Discovery`), JSON Schema validation, and the Global Hooks system.
    - Natively integrates the Authentication system (JWT, Refresh Token) and Security (MFA Gatekeeper).
    - **The container of a request**: hands every request `req.control`, and `req.tenant` where tenancy is declared. Two distinct types, no ambient fallback, and a call with neither throws.
2.  **`@volcanicminds/backend/db` (Data Layer)**
    - Drizzle underneath, and the subpath says so nowhere on purpose: in v4 it was `/typeorm`, so the ORM was
      part of the public API and replacing it was a breaking change for every consumer.
    - Introduces **"Magic Queries"**: a translation engine that turns a query string (filters, sort, pagination,
      boolean logic) into SQL — and answers **400 with a code** wherever v4 degraded into a different query.
    - Owns the framework's own tables, per-tenant containers, and versioned migrations.
    - **Optional and decoupled, not bundled into the core**: its dependencies (`drizzle-orm`, `bcrypt`, and `pg`
      or `better-sqlite3`/`@libsql/client`) are *optional peer dependencies*, so a project using only the HTTP
      core never installs them. The boundary is **enforced in CI**: the core may not import `lib/database/**`,
      and the data layer may import only *types* from the core. It is also **replaceable** — the managers are
      values you hand to `startServer()`, so an alternative implementation is a parameter. Full reference in
      [Part 3](#part-3-magic-queries--data-access), `docs/CONFIGURATION_V5.md` and `docs/SCHEMA_V5.md`.
3.  **`@volcanicminds/tools` (Utilities)**
    - A _tree-shakeable_ support library.
    - Provides standardized tools for Logger, Mailer, and MFA/OTP code generation.

### Architectural Principles

Every line of code in the project must adhere to these principles:

- **Thin Controllers ("Adapters"):** Controllers contain no business logic. Their only job is to normalize input (`req.data()`), resolve the container (`dataContext(req)`) and the caller's context, call a Service, and return the response.
- **Fat Services ("Business Logic"):** All logic, transactions, and data security controls reside here. Services do not know about `req` or `res` — they are **bound to a container** (`service.on(handle)`) and refuse to work without one.
- **Secure by Default:** Data access is never direct. It always passes through methods taking a context, and the security filter travels as `extraWhere`, AND-ed after everything the URL asked for.
- **No silent recovery:** a missing container, a failed audit write, an operator the engine cannot honour — each one is an error. Widening a scope to make a call succeed is the class of defect v5 was rewritten to remove.

### The "Globals" Pattern

Unlike architectures that use explicit Dependency Injection everywhere, the Volcanic Stack injects certain key utilities into the Node.js `global scope` during bootstrap. This drastically reduces circular imports and speeds up development.

- **`log`**: Pino Logger instance. Available everywhere.
- **`config`**: configuration loaded at startup, by `preload()`.
- **`roles`**, **`systemRoles`**: the two role catalogues, kept separate on purpose (T-4.1).
- **`t`**: the i18n instance.

**What is NOT global any more, and must never be generated:** `global.entity`, `global.repository`
and `global.connection`. All three were ways to reach a container without being given one, and
that is exactly how a request ended up reading another tenant's schema (defects D-01, D-06). A
container arrives on the request or it does not arrive; there is nothing ambient to fall back on.
The environment reader (`lib/util/env.ts`) is the one place a `process.env` value is turned into a
setting, so a documented variable cannot end up read by nobody — which happened anyway, to four of
them, until T-9.4 (defect D-11b).

---

## 1.2 Project Structure

The framework uses an **autodiscovery** system based on `glob` patterns. Adhering to the folder structure is mandatory for routes, entities, and configurations to be loaded.

```bash
./
├── .env                    # Environment variables (SECRETS)
├── package.json            # type: "module" (ESM), engines: node >= 24
├── tsconfig.json           # target: "ES2022", module: "NodeNext"
├── index.ts                # Entry Point (Bootstrap)
├── types                   # Custom TypeScript definitions
│   └── index.d.ts          # Global types extension (FastifyRequest, UserContext)
└── src
    ├── api                 # FUNCTIONAL MODULES (Domain Driven)
    │   └── [domain_name]   # e.g., "orders", "users"
    │       ├── controller  # Control logic (HTTP handling)
    │       │   └── [name].ts
    │       └── routes.ts   # Endpoint definition, Swagger, and Middleware
    ├── config              # GLOBAL CONFIGURATIONS
    │   ├── general.ts      # Framework config, AND the `control` / `tenants` blocks
    │   ├── plugins.ts      # Fastify Plugins (CORS, Helmet, RateLimit)
    │   ├── roles.ts        # Static RBAC Role definition
    │   └── tracking.ts     # Automatic Audit Log configuration
    ├── schema              # YOUR TABLES (Drizzle), built per container
    │   ├── pg.ts           # the factory: appTables(schemaName)
    │   ├── index.ts        # tablesFor(handle), cached by locator
    │   └── entry/          # static modules drizzle-kit generates from
    ├── services            # BUSINESS LOGIC (Service Layer)
    ├── schemas             # JSON SCHEMAS (Validation & Swagger Override)
    ├── hooks               # GLOBAL HOOKS
    ├── schedules           # CRON JOBS (*.job.ts)
    └── utils               # Helper functions

# and, beside src/:
├── migrations
│   ├── control/{pg,sqlite}   # your migrations for the control plane
│   └── tenant/{pg,sqlite}    # your migrations for a tenant container
└── drizzle.config.ts         # how they are generated
```

`src/config/database.ts` is **gone**: where the data lives is declared in `config/general.ts`,
in two blocks that cannot contradict each other. `src/entities` is gone with TypeORM.

---

## 1.3 Bootstrapping (`index.ts`)

Three steps, and the order is not a style choice.

```typescript
'use strict'

import { preload, start as startServer } from '@volcanicminds/backend'
import { start as startDataLayer } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'
// The MFA adapter from tools (a concrete implementation you own)
import { mfaAdapter } from './src/services/mfa.adapter.js'

const start = async () => {
  // 1. Read config/general.ts into global.config.
  //
  //    NOT optional, and forgetting it raises NOTHING: the data layer reads the `control` and
  //    `tenants` blocks from global.config, so out of order it finds no configuration and falls
  //    back to its own defaults — a different database, reached without an error. `startServer`
  //    calls preload() too, but by then the pool is already open against the wrong host.
  await preload()

  // 2. Open the data layer. It returns the managers plus `provider`, `migrations` and
  //    `migrateTenants`. They are values you own, not singletons imported from a subpath.
  const layer = await startDataLayer()

  // 3. Bring the control plane to the schema this code expects. In production this is a deploy
  //    step (`npm run db:migrate`); here it makes a clean machine work.
  await layer.migrations.apply({ locator: process.env.DB_SCHEMA || 'public' })

  // 4. Start the server with those managers as its decorators, plus anything of your own.
  await startServer({ ...layer, mfaManager: mfaAdapter })
}

start().catch((err) => {
  console.error('Fatal Error during startup:', err)
  process.exit(1)
})
```

**With no database at all** it is one line: `await startServer()`. The core falls back to
Null-Object managers, `/auth` reports that it is not implemented, and everything that does not
need a row keeps working.

**What changed from v4.** `startDatabase(config)` took the configuration as an argument and
populated `global.entity` / `global.connection`; the managers were module-level singletons
imported from `@volcanicminds/backend/typeorm`. None of that exists. There is no ambient
connection to populate, and the managers are returned rather than imported — which is what makes
swapping one a parameter instead of a patch.

---

## 1.4 Where the data lives (`config/general.ts`)

Two declared blocks, and no flag. `control` says where the platform's own data is; **declaring
`tenants` is what turns tenancy on**, so a flag and a strategy can no longer contradict each
other — in v4 they could, and the `resolver` that was documented was not the one that ran (D-11).

```typescript
// src/config/general.ts
export default {
  name: 'general',
  options: {
    control: {
      engine: 'postgres',                 // 'postgres' | 'sqlite' | 'libsql'
      url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,      // or the discrete DB_* variables
      schema: process.env.DB_SCHEMA || 'public',   // Postgres only: explicit, never inferred
      pool: { max: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_MAX) || 10, idleTimeoutMs: 30_000 }
    },

    // Absent = single tenant. This is most projects.
    tenants: {
      strategy: 'schema',                 // 'schema' | 'container'
      engine: 'postgres',
      resolver: 'header',                 // 'header' | 'subdomain'
      headerKey: 'x-tenant-id',
      containers: { maxOpen: 20, idleTimeoutMs: 300_000, poolMax: 2 }
    }
  }
}
```

The merge over the framework defaults is **deep**: declaring one key inside `tenants` no longer
erases its siblings, which in v4 is how `multi_tenant: { enabled: true }` silently discarded the
resolver (D-21).

**The four supported combinations**, checked at boot by the capability matrix. Anything else logs
fatal and exits — a deployment the framework cannot isolate must not start, because the
alternative is starting and mixing two customers' rows.

| `control.engine` | `tenants` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `postgres` | absent | single tenant |
| `postgres` | `strategy: 'schema'`, `engine: 'postgres'` | many tenants, one database, a schema each |
| `postgres` | `strategy: 'container'`, `engine: 'postgres'` | one database per tenant |
| `postgres` | `strategy: 'container'`, `engine: 'sqlite' \| 'libsql'` | one file per tenant |
| `sqlite` / `libsql` | absent, or `strategy: 'container'` | serverless processes: CLI, agents, desktop |

**No naming strategy to configure.** Columns are declared explicitly (`text('first_name')`), so
`snake_case` in the database and `camelCase` in TypeScript is written down rather than derived
from a convention that a future version of an ORM might read differently.

**PGlite and MongoDB are not deployment engines.** PGlite exposes a single connection, so it
cannot isolate anything under concurrency — which is the entire class of defect v5 was rewritten
to remove; it survives only as a test double. MongoDB is removed outright: its multi-tenant path
was **fail-open**, logging a warning and then working on the whole database with no isolation
(D-04).

## 1.5 Environment Variables (Reference)

An example `.env` for production.

| Variable                       | Description                                                             | Required | Default             |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------: | ------------------- |
| `NODE_ENV`                     | The application environment.                                            |    No    | `development`       |
| `HOST`                         | The host address for the server. Use `0.0.0.0` for Docker.              |    No    | `0.0.0.0`           |
| `PORT`                         | The port for the server to listen on.                                   |    No    | `2230`              |
| `JWT_SECRET`                   | Secret key for signing JWTs.                                            | **Yes**  |                     |
| `JWT_EXPIRES_IN`               | Expiration time for JWTs (e.g., `5d`, `12h`).                           |    No    | `5d`                |
| `JWT_REFRESH`                  | Enable refresh tokens.                                                  |    No    | `true`              |
| `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET`           | Secret key for signing refresh tokens.                                  | **Yes**¹ |                     |
| `JWT_REFRESH_EXPIRES_IN`       | Expiration time for refresh tokens.                                     |    No    | `180d`              |
| `LOG_LEVEL`                    | Logging verbosity (`trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `fatal`). |    No    | `info`              |
| `LOG_COLORIZE`                 | Enable colorized log output.                                            |    No    | `true`              |
| `LOG_TIMESTAMP`                | Enable timestamps in logs.                                              |    No    | `true`              |
| `LOG_TIMESTAMP_READABLE`       | Use a human-readable timestamp format.                                  |    No    | `true`              |
| `LOG_FASTIFY`                  | Enable Fastify's built-in logger.                                       |    No    | `false`             |
| `SWAGGER`                      | Enable Swagger/OpenAPI documentation.                                   |    No    | `true`              |
| `SWAGGER_HOST`                 | The base URL for the API, used in Swagger docs.                         |    No    | `localhost:2230`    |
| `SWAGGER_TITLE`                | The title of the API documentation.                                     |    No    | `API Documentation` |
| `SWAGGER_DESCRIPTION`          | The description for the API documentation.                              |    No    |                     |
| `SWAGGER_VERSION`              | The version of the API.                                                 |    No    | `0.1.0`             |
| `SWAGGER_PREFIX_URL`           | The path where Swagger UI is available.                                 |    No    | `/api-docs`         |
| `MFA_POLICY`                   | MFA Security Policy (`OPTIONAL`, `MANDATORY`, `ONE_WAY`)                |    No    | `OPTIONAL`          |
| `MFA_ADMIN_FORCED_RESET_EMAIL` | Admin email for emergency MFA reset                                     |    No    |                     |
| `MFA_ADMIN_FORCED_RESET_UNTIL` | ISO Date string until which the reset is active                         |    No    |                     |
| `HIDE_ERROR_DETAILS`           | Prevent error details (message) from being sent in response. Honoured by **every** error path, the `onError` hook included. |    No    | `true` (prod)       |
| `CORS_ORIGINS`                 | Comma-separated allowlist. **Required in production**: a wildcard that arrived by omission refuses the boot, and so does the wildcard-with-credentials pair. |  **Yes**²  |          |
| `MFA_DB_SECRET`                | Key the MFA secrets are encrypted with. Falls back to `JWT_SECRET`.     |    No    |                     |
| `ADMIN_EMAIL` / `ADMIN_PASSWORD` | Seeds the **first** identity, at boot and at no other time.           | **Yes**³ |                     |
| `DATABASE_URL`                 | Control-plane connection. Wins over the discrete `DB_*` variables.      |    No    |                     |
| `DB_SCHEMA`                    | Control-plane schema. Explicit, never inferred.                        |    No    | `public`            |
| `DB_POOL_MAX`                  | Control-plane pool size.                                                |    No    | `10`                |
| `BCRYPT_COST`                  | Password work factor. **Never below 12**, whatever is written. Measure it with `npm run tune`. |    No    | `12`  |
| `VOLCANIC_MAX_PAGE_SIZE`       | Upper clamp on `_pageSize`.                                             |    No    | `100`               |
| `TENANT_CONTAINERS_MAX_OPEN`   | LRU bound on live tenant containers.                                    |    No    | `20`                |
| `TENANT_CONTAINERS_DIR`        | Where per-tenant files live (file-per-container engines).               |    No    | `./data/tenants`    |
| `DESTRUCTION_TOKEN_TTL`        | Seconds a container-destruction request stays valid.                    |    No    | `600`               |
| `IMPERSONATION_TTL`            | Seconds an impersonation token lasts. Hard maximum 14400.               |    No    | `1800`              |

¹ Required if `JWT_REFRESH` is enabled.
² Required in production.
³ Read only at boot, to seed the first identity. With no identity and no `ADMIN_EMAIL`, startup fails fast.

**Removed in v5**, and not renamed: `START_DB` and `DB_SYNCHRONIZE_SCHEMA_AT_STARTUP` (the schema
is versioned migrations now, applied as a deploy step), `VOLCANIC_CUSTOM_QUERY_OPERATORS` (the
`:raw` operator is gone), `VOLCANIC_CASE_INSENSITIVE_DEFAULT` (case sensitivity is a property of
the operator, so one URL cannot mean two things on two servers).

> Four of the variables above — `VOLCANIC_MAX_PAGE_SIZE`, `TENANT_CONTAINERS_MAX_OPEN`,
> `TENANT_CONTAINERS_DIR`, `DESTRUCTION_TOKEN_TTL` — were documented from the start of v5 and
> read by **nobody** until T-9.4 found it, which is defect D-11 in another shape. If you are
> generating configuration, the rule the framework holds itself to is: the declared default is
> what the code does, and no field is typed, documented and never read.

---

## 1.7 Single vs Multi-Tenant Architecture

Both are supported, and the difference a consumer sees is **one field**: `req.tenant` is present
or it is not. `const container = dataContext(req)` is the whole idiom, so the same
service code serves both.

- **Single tenant** (default): no `tenants` block. The application's data lives in the control
  plane, and `req.tenant` is never set.
- **Multi tenant**: declare the block. **Declaring it is what enables tenancy** — there is no
  `enabled` flag that can contradict the strategy beside it.

```typescript
// src/config/general.ts
export default {
  options: {
    tenants: {
      strategy: 'schema',        // 'schema' | 'container'
      engine: 'postgres',
      resolver: 'header',        // 'header' | 'subdomain'. No 'query': a tenant id in a URL
      headerKey: 'x-tenant-id'   // lands in access logs, Referer headers and browser history
    }
  }
}
```

**How the tenant is chosen, and it is not the header.** The tenant comes from the token's `tid`
claim whenever there is a token. The resolver is consulted only for requests that carry none —
login and public routes — and only the configured one is read, never both. In v4 the header
decided always, the `resolver` option was typed and documented and never read (D-11), and the
anti-spoofing check meant to catch a mismatch compared a field the entity did not have, in a hook
that ran too early (D-03). It never fired.

**What isolation is, mechanically.** A container is chosen by **qualifying the table objects**,
not by `SET search_path` on a pooled connection. Drizzle prints the schema name into the SQL, so
choosing a container is choosing an object, nothing is left on the session, and nothing has to be
reset before the connection goes back to the pool. That last clause is defect D-01 designed out:
in v4 the reset was written twice, in the wrong order, and never ran — so a tenant's `search_path`
survived in the pool and a control-plane route could list another customer's users.

| Situation | Answer |
|---|---|
| nothing names a tenant, and tenancy is on | 400 `TENANT_REQUIRED` |
| the tenant is unknown **or suspended** | 404 — the same answer for both, so the registry cannot be probed from outside |
| the token's `tid` disagrees with the resolved tenant | 403 `TENANT_MISMATCH` |
| a control token inside a tenant, or the reverse | 403 `SCOPE_MISMATCH` |
| the container is behind its schema version | 503 `SCHEMA_BEHIND`, for that tenant alone |

Here is a full configuration file:

```properties
# --- Server ---
NODE_ENV=production
HOST=0.0.0.0
PORT=2230
APP_NAME=volcanic-sample-backend
HIDE_ERROR_DETAILS=true

# --- Database ---
# One URL wins over the discrete variables. The schema is explicit, never inferred.
DATABASE_URL=postgres://admin:secret_password@10.0.0.5:5432/db_prod
DB_SCHEMA=public
DB_POOL_MAX=10
# Measured, not copied: npm run tune (docs/TUNING.md)
BCRYPT_COST=12
TENANT_CONTAINERS_MAX_OPEN=20

# The schema is applied by `npm run db:migrate`, a deploy step. There is no
# DB_SYNCHRONIZE_SCHEMA_AT_STARTUP: a restart that rewrites the shape of a production
# database is not a feature.

# --- Auth & Security ---
# Required in production: the origins allowed to call this API.
CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com
# Seeds the FIRST identity, at boot and at no other time.
ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.com
# Generate with: openssl rand -base64 64
JWT_SECRET=super_secret_key_change_me
JWT_EXPIRES_IN=1h
JWT_REFRESH=true
JWT_REFRESH_SECRET=super_secret_refresh_key_change_me
JWT_REFRESH_EXPIRES_IN=30d
MFA_DB_SECRET=a_third_secret_at_least_32_characters

# MFA
MFA_POLICY=OPTIONAL
MFA_ADMIN_FORCED_RESET_EMAIL=admin@example.com
MFA_ADMIN_FORCED_RESET_UNTIL=2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z

# --- API Documentation ---
SWAGGER=true
SWAGGER_HOST=localhost:2230
SWAGGER_TITLE=API Documentation
SWAGGER_DESCRIPTION=List of available APIs and schemas to use
SWAGGER_VERSION=0.1.0
SWAGGER_PREFIX_URL=/api-docs

# --- Logging ---
LOG_LEVEL=info
LOG_COLORIZE=false
LOG_TIMESTAMP=true
LOG_TIMESTAMP_READABLE=true
LOG_FASTIFY=false
```

---

## 1.6 Fastify Plugin Configuration (Rate Limit, Raw Body, Static)

You can enable and configure native Fastify plugins via the `src/config/plugins.ts` file.

### Raw Body

Useful for webhooks (e.g., Stripe) that require the raw payload for signature validation.

```typescript
{
  name: 'rawBody',
  enable: true,
  options: {
    global: false, // If true, adds rawBody to all requests (memory intensive)
    runFirst: true // Parses before other hooks
  }
}
```

If `global: false`, you can enable it on a single route in `routes.ts`:

```typescript
config: {
  rawBody: true
}
```

### Rate Limit

Protects the API from abuse. Global configuration in `plugins.ts`:

```typescript
{
  name: 'rateLimit',
  enable: true,
  options: {
    global: true,
    max: 100,
    timeWindow: 60000 // 1 minute
  }
}
```

You can override limits per route by defining the `rateLimit` object in the route definition.

### Static Files (optional)

An **opt-in** named `static` plugin serves a static folder (e.g. a `public/uploads` directory in dev; typically
fronted by nginx/CDN in prod) via `@fastify/static`. Disabled by default. `@fastify/static` is dynamically
imported, so consumers that don't enable it needn't install it.

```typescript
{
  name: 'static',
  enable: true,
  // @fastify/static options: { root, prefix?, decorateReply? }
  options: { root: '/abs/path/to/public', prefix: '/public/' }
}
```

`options` may also be an **array** of option objects to expose multiple roots/prefixes; the framework sets
`decorateReply: true` only on the first mount (subsequent mounts get `false` to avoid re-decorating `reply`).

## 1.6b Per-route Response Cache (optional)

An **opt-in**, in-memory response cache for read-heavy, slow-changing endpoints (e.g. a public storefront).
Declare it per route in `routes.ts` — or once at the file level in `config.cache` (inherited by every route in
that file, overridable per route):

```typescript
// cache: true | <ttlSeconds> | { enabled?, ttl?, keyGroup?, invalidates? }
routes: [
  { method: 'GET', path: '/', roles: [roles.public], handler: 'public.vehicles',
    cache: { ttl: 3600 } },                       // cache this GET for 1h (key-group = api folder)
  { method: 'PUT', path: '/:id', roles: [roles.admin], handler: 'vehicle.update',
    cache: { invalidates: ['public'] } }          // on 2xx, flush the 'public' key-group
]
```

Semantics:

- Only **GET** responses with a **2xx** status are cached. The read is a `preHandler` (runs **after** the
  auth/roles onRequest hook) that short-circuits on a hit; the write is an `onSend` capturing the serialized
  body plus the `v-*` pagination headers (replayed on a hit). Mutations are never cached.
- **Scope-safe key** = `keyGroup :: tenant | subject | roles :: METHOD url`. Anonymous/`public` callers share
  an entry; authenticated calls are isolated per subject/tenant/role — a cached response is never leaked across
  them. Caching is skipped when multi-tenant is on but the tenant is missing.
- **Store**: internal **LRU + TTL** (no dependency). Global defaults live in `general.ts`
  `options.cache = { enabled: true, ttl: 3600, maxEntries: 1000 }`; the effective config is logged at startup.
- **`keyGroup`** defaults to the api folder (area), e.g. `src/api/public/*` → `public`. Override it to
  share/segment a group across folders.
- **Invalidation** is by key-group: declaratively with `cache.invalidates: string | string[]` on a mutating
  route, or imperatively:

```typescript
import { invalidateCache } from '@volcanicminds/backend'
invalidateCache('public')          // flush one key-group
invalidateCache(['public','brands'])
invalidateCache()                  // flush everything
// also available as global.cache.invalidate/flushAll/del/stats
```

**File-level default (inheritance).** `cache` may also live on the file-level `config`, inherited by every route
in that file (a per-route `cache` overrides it). The common adoption pattern:

```typescript
// src/api/public/routes.ts — cache every GET under the 'public' key-group
config: { title: 'Public', controller: 'controller', cache: { ttl: 3600 } }

// src/api/vehicles/routes.ts — DON'T cache admin (per-user) responses, just flush the
// storefront on every successful mutation
config: { title: 'Vehicles', controller: 'controller', cache: { enabled: false, invalidates: ['public'] } }
```

Full guide (guards, key scoping, LRU/TTL store, caveats): **docs/CACHE.md**.

---

# Part 2: Your Own Tables

> **Ported from v4.** TypeORM entities, `@Entity`, `@Column`, `BaseEntity`, `global.entity` and
> `.e.ts` files are gone. Tables are Drizzle, they are declared by the project that owns them,
> and they are built **per container**. `docs/SCHEMA_V5.md` is the contract.

## 2.1 The shape of a table module

A **factory**, not a module of constants. This is the single most important thing to get right,
and the reason is mechanical rather than stylistic: Drizzle prints the schema name into the SQL
it builds — `select … from "tenant_acme"."product"` — so a table object **is** the choice of
container. Building them per locator is what makes tenancy work without touching `search_path`
on a pooled connection.

```typescript
// src/tables/pg.ts
import { pgSchema, pgTable, text, timestamp, index, check } from 'drizzle-orm/pg-core'
import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm'
import { uuidv7 } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'

const stamps = () => ({
  createdAt: timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
  updatedAt: timestamp('updated_at', { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
  deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at', { withTimezone: true })
})

// `public` is left unqualified because Drizzle refuses `pgSchema('public')`; the adapter pins
// `search_path` on the connection once, at connect time, so unqualified names still resolve to
// one place and to the same place for every request.
const tableFactory = (schemaName: string): typeof pgTable =>
  (schemaName && schemaName !== 'public' ? pgSchema(schemaName).table : pgTable) as typeof pgTable

export function appTables(schemaName: string) {
  const table = tableFactory(schemaName)

  const product = table(
    'product',
    {
      id: text('id').primaryKey().$defaultFn(uuidv7),
      name: text('name'),
      // A text column with a CHECK, not a Postgres `enum` type: adding a value to a native enum
      // is a DDL migration that takes a lock, and this list changes with the business.
      status: text('status', { enum: ['draft', 'published'] }).notNull().default('draft'),
      ...stamps()
    },
    (t) => [index('product_name_idx').on(t.name), check('product_status_check', sql`"status" in ('draft', 'published')`)]
  )

  return { product }
}

export type AppTables = ReturnType<typeof appTables>
```

**Conventions**, applied everywhere and declared rather than derived:

- `snake_case` in the database, `camelCase` in TypeScript, **written out**. No naming strategy to
  configure and no convention a future ORM version might read differently.
- `timestamptz`, never a naive timestamp. On SQLite the same value is an integer of epoch
  **milliseconds**, always UTC — no local time ever reaches the database.
- Identifiers minted in process with `uuidv7()`: time-ordered, so inserts stay local in the
  b-tree instead of scattering, and a row carries its creation instant. v4 looked up a free id
  with a `do/while` around a SELECT — a round trip per insert, to solve a collision that does not
  happen (D-28).
- `deletedAt` is what makes a soft delete: the query layer hides those rows automatically unless a
  route declares `allowWithDeleted`.

## 2.2 Resolving tables for the request's container

```typescript
// src/tables/index.ts
import type { DataHandle } from '@volcanicminds/backend'
import { access } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'
import { appTables, type AppTables } from './pg.js'

const cache = new Map<string, AppTables>()

export function tablesFor(handle: DataHandle): AppTables {
  const { dialect, locator } = access(handle, 'tablesFor')
  if (dialect !== 'postgres') throw new Error(`this project's tables are Postgres; container speaks '${dialect}'`)

  const key = locator || 'public'
  if (!cache.has(key)) cache.set(key, appTables(key))
  return cache.get(key)!
}
```

**The cache key must be the locator.** Two tenants differ in nothing else, and a cache that
ignored it would hand tenant B the object naming tenant A's schema — which is defect D-01 rebuilt
inside application code. Two lines well spent.

## 2.3 Never redefine a framework table

The framework owns `user`, `token`, `change`, `migration` and, in the control plane, `tenant`,
`system_user`, `impersonation`, `destruction_request`. **Do not extend them.**

In v4 the way to add `firstName` to a user was to subclass the framework's `User` entity. In v5
those fields go in a table of your own, keyed by `user.id`:

```typescript
const userProfile = table('user_profile', {
  userId: text('user_id').primaryKey(),
  firstName: text('first_name'),
  lastName: text('last_name'),
  ...stamps()
})
```

No foreign key is declared, deliberately: the framework owns `user` and migrates it, so a
constraint pointing into a table this project does not migrate would make the two sets of
migrations depend on each other's order.

The reason for the rule is not tidiness. A framework table redefined by a consumer collides with
every future framework migration, and the collision arrives **at upgrade time, on a deployment
already in production** — the worst moment and the hardest to attribute.

## 2.4 Enums and domain vocabularies

A frozen list plus a string union, and the list is what the check constraint and the JSON schema
are built from — so the values live in one place and a new one cannot enter the type without
appearing in the validation.

```typescript
export const PARTNER_TYPES = ['client', 'supplier', 'contact'] as const
export type PartnerType = (typeof PARTNER_TYPES)[number]
```

A TypeScript `enum` would give a second source of truth that the database never sees. A `CHECK`
keeps the database honest anyway: a union does not survive a `psql` session.

## 2.5 Relations

Declared where they are used — in the query — rather than as eager/lazy metadata on the table.
A join is a decision about one endpoint's cost, and putting it on the model makes it a decision
about every endpoint at once. v4's `eager: true` is the reason a list endpoint could quietly
become six joins.

Routes that allow joining declare which relations are joinable (`allowedRelations` in
`QueryOptions`), and a relation a route does not allow answers **400
`QUERY_RELATION_NOT_ALLOWED`** rather than being silently ignored.

## 2.6 Migrations own the shape

There is no `synchronize: true` and no `POST /tool/synchronize-schemas`. The schema is committed
SQL, generated by `drizzle-kit`, applied in order, and recorded **inside each container**:

```sh
npm run db:generate          # control, Postgres
npm run db:generate:tenant   # tenant, Postgres
npm run db:migrate           # apply — a deploy step, not a boot step
```

Two sets (`control`, `tenant`) because the two have different lives, and two dialects (`pg`,
`sqlite`) because the SQL genuinely differs: `timestamp with time zone` against an integer of
epoch milliseconds, `USING btree` against nothing at all. Translating one into the other at apply
time would put a statement **nobody has read** in front of a customer's data, which is the whole
reason migrations are committed SQL. The two dialects of a set carry the **same names**, and
`npm run check:migration-sets` fails when one gains a migration the other does not.

Forward only: `drizzle-kit` generates no `down`, and a `down` on a destructive migration restores
the form and not the data — a promise that fails exactly when it is called on. Reversibility lives
in expand/contract releases.

## 2.7 Modeling best practices

- One table per thing the business names. Resist the urge to widen a framework table.
- Soft delete with `deletedAt` where history matters; the query layer hides those rows for you.
- Put the check constraint in the database, not only in the type.
- Index what you filter on, and say why in a comment — an index nobody can justify is an index
  nobody dares remove.
- Never store a tenant identifier in a tenant's own table. The container **is** the tenancy; a
  column repeating it is a second source of truth and the first thing to drift.

---

# Part 3: Magic Queries & Data Access

> **Ported from v4.** The grammar changed: reserved parameters carry an underscore, sorting is
> `_sort=-field`, operator names lost the `s` suffix and gained `i`, ranges use `..`, and `:raw`
> is gone. The full v4 → v5 correspondence table is `docs/MAGIC_QUERY_V5.md` §9. Nothing degrades
> silently any more: every shape v4 answered differently is now a **400 with a code**.

## 3.1 Translation Layer: URL to SQL

`HTTP query string` → `parseQuery()` → SQL, built for the dialect the handle speaks.

```typescript
// src/api/products/controller/product.ts
import { FastifyReply, FastifyRequest } from '@volcanicminds/backend'
import { access, executeFind } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'
import { tablesFor } from '../../../tables/index.js'

export async function find(req: FastifyRequest, reply: FastifyReply) {
  // The container this request works on. No fallback: a route that arrives here without one has
  // lost its context, and reading "whichever container the pool last touched" is the defect v5
  // exists to remove.
  const container = dataContext(req)

  const { db, dialect } = access(container)
  const { product } = tablesFor(container)

  const { headers, records } = await executeFind({ db }, product, req.data(), {
    dialect,
    sensitiveFields: ['secret'],       // never returned, and never filterable either
    extraWhere: onlyMine(req)          // row-level security the URL cannot argue with
  })

  return reply.headers(headers).send(records)   // v-total, v-count, v-page, v-pageSize, v-pageCount
}
```

## 3.2 Reserved parameters

Underscore-prefixed, so a column called `page` is a column and not a directive — in v4 it could
not be both.

| | |
|---|---|
| `_page` | 1-based. `_page=0` answers 400 `QUERY_INVALID_PAGE` |
| `_pageSize` | default 25, clamped to `VOLCANIC_MAX_PAGE_SIZE` (100). The applied value comes back in `v-pageSize` |
| `_sort` | comma-separated, a leading `-` is descending: `_sort=-createdAt,name`. An unknown field answers 400 |
| `_fields` | projection: `_fields=id,name` |
| `_relations` | relations to join, dot notation for depth |
| `_logic` | boolean expression over aliased conditions |
| `_withDeleted` | only where the route declares `allowWithDeleted`, otherwise 400 |

Removed: `page`, `pageSize`, `sort`, `skip`, `take`. `skip`/`take` do not come back under another
name — page and page size describe the same thing, and having both invites two answers to one
question.

## 3.3 Filter operator reference

`field[:operator][alias]=value`. Omitting the operator means `:eq`.

**The naming rule has no exceptions**: the base form is **case-sensitive**, the suffix `i` makes
it insensitive, the prefix `n` negates it. In v4 the base form was insensitive or not depending on
`VOLCANIC_CASE_INSENSITIVE_DEFAULT`, so one URL returned different results on two servers of the
same product. That switch is removed; case sensitivity is visible in the URL.

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `:eq` `:neq` `:eqi` `:neqi` | equality, sensitive and insensitive |
| `:in` `:nin` | set membership, comma-separated. An empty element (`a,,b`) answers 400 |
| `:gt` `:ge` `:lt` `:le` | comparison, on numbers/dates/timestamps |
| `:between` `:nbetween` | inclusive range, written **`from..to`** |
| `:contains` `:starts` `:ends` `:like` (+ `i`/`n` variants) | text matching |
| `:null` | `:null=true` / `:null=false` |
| `:empty` | `= ''` / `<> ''`, text columns only |
| `:arrayContains` `:arrayContainedBy` `:arrayOverlaps` | Postgres arrays |
| `:jsonHasKey` `:jsonHasAnyKey` `:jsonHasAllKeys` | Postgres JSONB |

**Gone, with no replacement:** `:raw` (it interpolated a caller's SQL fragment; with a tenant
container in reach that is a way across the boundary — D-12), the `s` suffix family
(`:eqs`, `:containss`…, where "strict" is now the base form), `:notNull` (use `:null=false`) and
`:isEmpty`/`:isNotEmpty` (use `:empty=true|false`) — three operators that duplicated two meanings,
two of which ignored their value entirely.

**Escaping is mandatory and automatic.** For `contains`, `starts` and `ends` the value is user
data: `%`, `_` and the escape character are escaped before the pattern is built, and the query is
emitted with `ESCAPE '\'`. In v4 they were not, so `amount:contains=50%` quietly searched for
anything starting with `50`. For `:like` the wildcards are the caller's intent and stay.

**Coercion follows the column, not the string.** `code:eq=0042` on a text column stays the string
`0042`; on a date column all digits mean epoch **milliseconds**, because `new Date('1500')` would
otherwise mean the year 1500 and a client sending a timestamp would get eight centuries of
nonsense back with no error. A value the column cannot hold answers 400 `QUERY_INVALID_VALUE`.

Field names are the ones the **response** uses — `createdAt`, not `created_at`. A client filters
on what it reads back.

## 3.4 Boolean logic (`_logic`)

```text
# active OR expensive
?status:eq[a]=active&price:ge[b]=100&_logic=a OR b

# (active from Italy) OR (pending from Germany)
?status:eq[s1]=active&country:eq[c1]=IT&status:eq[s2]=pending&country:eq[c2]=DE&_logic=(s1 AND c1) OR (s2 AND c2)
```

Grammar: aliases, `AND`/`OR`/`NOT` (case-insensitive), parentheses. Nothing else. Limits, all
enforced and all answering 400: expression length 512, nesting depth 8, 32 aliases.

When `_logic` is present **every** condition must carry an alias and appear in the expression. The
framework refuses a half-aliased query rather than guessing which conditions it meant.

**What v4 hid and v5 reports:**

| Situation | v4 | v5 |
|---|---|---|
| unparseable expression | fell back to `AND` of everything, silently returning a different result set | 400 `QUERY_LOGIC_INVALID` |
| depth or length exceeded | recursion error caught, same silent fallback | 400 `QUERY_LOGIC_TOO_COMPLEX` |
| alias used and never defined | condition ignored | 400 `QUERY_LOGIC_UNKNOWN_ALIAS` |
| condition defined and never used | condition silently dropped | 400 `QUERY_LOGIC_UNUSED_ALIAS` |
| `_logic` present, some conditions unaliased | ambiguous | 400 `QUERY_LOGIC_MISSING_ALIAS` |
| the same field twice with no alias | kept the last one | 400 `QUERY_DUPLICATE_CONDITION` |

## 3.5 Pagination and sorting

`_page` is 1-based, `_pageSize` is clamped, and the applied values come back in headers:
`v-total`, `v-count`, `v-page`, `v-pageSize`, `v-pageCount`. A client paginates from the headers,
never from a count it computed.

`_sort=-createdAt,name` — descending on the first, ascending on the second. An unknown field
answers 400 rather than being skipped, because a skipped sort field returns the right rows in the
wrong order, which looks like data and is not.

## 3.6 Global search

There is no `q` parameter. A console or client that wants "search everywhere" builds the OR
itself, over the fields the manifest declares searchable, and combines it with any other filters
through `_logic`:

```text
?name:containsi[c0]=mario&email:containsi[c1]=mario&status:in[c2]=a,b&_logic=(c0 OR c1) AND c2
```

`@volcanicminds/admin` does exactly this (`src/engine/magic-query.ts`). A `q` handled server-side
would need the server to know which of a consumer's fields are searchable, which is what the
manifest is for.

## 3.7 Security hardening

- **Sensitive fields are never returned and — new in v5 — never filterable.** `password`,
  `mfaSecret`, `resetPasswordToken`, `confirmationToken` by default; extend with
  `sensitiveFields` in `QueryOptions`. Filtering a hash is an oracle: it answers questions about a
  value nobody is allowed to read. v4 allowed it.
- **`extraWhere` is AND-ed last**, after everything the URL asked for and `_logic` included, so no
  expression a client can write reaches around a row-level-security rule.
- **Operators an engine cannot honour answer 400** `QUERY_OPERATOR_NOT_SUPPORTED_BY_ENGINE`,
  naming the operator and the engine — never silently ignored, never emulated with a slower
  approximation that returns different rows.
- **`:raw` is removed**, and so is the environment flag that gated it.

## 3.8 Data layer API reference

| | |
|---|---|
| `start(options?)` | opens the data layer; returns the managers, `provider`, `migrations`, `migrateTenants`, `shutdown`. Reads `global.config.options` when called with nothing |
| `access(handle)` | the inside of a handle: `db`, `dialect`, `tenantId`, `locator`, `execute`, `transaction` |
| `executeFind(handle, table, params, options)` | find and count in one call: `{ records, headers }` |
| `executeCount(handle, table, params, options)` | how many rows match, ignoring the page |
| `parseQuery(table, params, options)` | the translation alone, for a query you assemble yourself |
| `uuidv7()` | a time-ordered identifier, minted in process |
| `encrypt` / `decrypt` | AES-256-GCM, per-record derivation. **Async** in v5: the v4 pair blocked the event loop for 82 ms per call, on the MFA login path (D-14) |
| `migrationSets()`, `migrationDialect(engine)` | where migrations are read from, per set and dialect |

`QueryOptions`: `dialect`, `sensitiveFields`, `maxPageSize`, `defaultPageSize`,
`allowWithDeleted`, `allowedRelations`, `logicLimits`, `extraWhere`.

Replaced from v4: `executeFindQuery` → `executeFind`, `executeCountQuery` → `executeCount`,
`applyQuery` → `parseQuery`. `useWhere` and `useOrder` have no successor — `parseQuery` returns
`where` and `orderBy` separately.

## 3.9 Standalone usage

`parseQuery` takes a table and a plain object, so it runs outside the HTTP core:

```typescript
import { parseQuery } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'
const { where, orderBy, limit, offset } = parseQuery(product, req.query, { dialect: 'postgres' })
```

## 3.10 Multi-tenancy in one paragraph

There is nothing to switch. `switchContext` and `runInTenantContext` do not exist, because
choosing a container is not a session change: application code asks `dataContext(req)`,
and a background job **declares its plane** and receives the matching handle (Part 7.3). What made
the v4 helpers necessary — a global connection whose `search_path` had to be moved and moved back
— is the defect that was designed out.

## 3.11 Utility: password hash generation

```sh
node generate-hash.js 'MyS3cretP@ss'
# $2b$12$....
```

The work factor is `BCRYPT_COST` (default 12, never lower), and `npm run tune` measures the right
one for the machine that will run it. See `docs/TUNING.md`.

## 3.12 Local database setup (Docker)

```sh
docker run -d --name vm-pg \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=volcanic -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=volcanic -e POSTGRES_DB=volcanic \
  -p 5432:5432 postgres:16-alpine

npm run db:migrate
```

PGlite is **not** an option here: it exposes a single connection, so it cannot isolate anything
under concurrency, which is the class of defect the v5 data layer exists to remove. It survives
only as a test double.

---

# Part 4: API Layer (Routing & Controllers)

The API layer is the application entry point. Its responsibility is strictly limited to:

1.  **Receiving** the HTTP request.
2.  **Validating** input (via JSON Schema).
3.  **Verifying** authorization (via Middleware/Roles).
4.  **Delegating** processing to the Service Layer.
5.  **Responding** to the client.

## 4.1 Route Autodiscovery

The framework uses an **Automatic Loader** (`lib/loader/router.ts`) that scans the `src/api` folder at server startup. There is no central `app.ts` file where routes are manually registered.

### The Matching Rule

The loader looks for files matching the pattern: `src/api/**/routes.ts`.
Folder structure determines the URL prefix, unless overwritten in configuration.

**Mapping Examples:**

| File Path                     | Configuration  | Resulting URL |
| :---------------------------- | :------------- | :------------ |
| `src/api/users/routes.ts`     | `path: '/'`    | `/users/`     |
| `src/api/users/routes.ts`     | `path: '/:id'` | `/users/:id`  |
| `src/api/orders/v2/routes.ts` | `path: '/'`    | `/orders/v2/` |

---

## 4.2 `routes.ts` Configuration

Every functional module (e.g., `orders`, `auth`) must have a `routes.ts` file. This file is the "Single Source of Truth" for endpoint behavior and Swagger/OpenAPI documentation generation.

### File Structure

Here is a complete, commented example based on `src/api/orders/routes.ts`:

```typescript
import { roles } from '../../config/roles.js' // Import defined roles

export default {
  // 1. Module Global Configuration
  config: {
    title: 'Orders API', // Group name in Swagger
    description: 'Management of orders and jobs',
    controller: 'controller', // Subfolder where to look for handler files (default: 'controller')
    tags: ['orders'], // Tag for Swagger grouping
    enable: true // Switch to enable/disable the entire module
  },

  // 2. Route Definition
  routes: [
    {
      method: 'GET', // Verbs: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH
      path: '/:id', // Path relative to module (becomes /orders/:id)

      // --- Security Layer ---
      // RBAC: Only Admin and Manager can call this route.
      // If array is empty [], route is public (unless blocked by middleware).
      roles: [roles.admin, roles.manager],

      // Middleware Chain: Executed in order before handler.
      middlewares: ['global.isAuthenticated'],

      // --- Handler Mapping ---
      // Magic Syntax: 'filename.functionName'
      // Framework will look for file 'order.ts' in 'controller' folder
      // and execute exported function 'findOne'.
      handler: 'order.findOne',

      // --- Swagger & Validation ---
      config: {
        title: 'Find Order',
        description: 'Retrieves order detail',

        // JSON Schema References (Automatic Fastify Validation)
        // Names with # refer to globally loaded schemas in src/schemas
        params: { $ref: 'globalParamsSchema#' }, // Validates :id presence
        response: {
          200: {
            description: 'Success',
            $ref: 'orderSchema#' // Serializes response using this schema
          },
          404: { description: 'Order not found' }
        }
      }
    },

    // Example Creation Route
    {
      method: 'POST',
      path: '/',
      roles: [roles.admin],
      handler: 'order.create',
      middlewares: ['global.isAuthenticated'],
      config: {
        title: 'Create Order',
        // Body Validation
        body: { $ref: 'orderBodySchema#' },
        response: {
          200: { $ref: 'orderSchema#' }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

---

## 4.3 Controllers: Best Practices

Controllers in this stack must be **Thin**. They must not contain SQL queries, business logic, or external service calls.

### Standard Signature

Every handler is an async function:

```typescript
import { FastifyReply, FastifyRequest } from '@volcanicminds/backend'

export async function myHandler(req: FastifyRequest, reply: FastifyReply) {
  // ...
}
```

### 1. Input Normalization (`req.data()`)

Fastify separates `req.body` (POST/PUT) from `req.query` (GET).
The framework provides the `req.data()` helper which unifies both into a single object, allowing code agnostic to HTTP method.

```typescript
// Instead of: const data = req.body || req.query
const data = req.data()
```

### 2. Path Parameters (`req.parameters()`)

To access URL parameters (e.g., `/orders/:id`), use the helper:

```typescript
// Instead of: req.params
const { id } = req.parameters()
```

### 3. The container, and the caller

Two things every data-touching controller resolves, and neither is ambient.

```typescript
// src/utils/context.ts — yours, not the framework's
import type { FastifyRequest } from '@volcanicminds/backend'

// The container is NOT one of the two. `dataContext` is exported by the framework, and
// writing your own `req.tenant ?? req.control` in its place is the one thing to avoid: it
// gives a tenant route that lost its container the control plane instead of an error.
export { dataContext as container } from '@volcanicminds/backend'

/** What the application knows about the caller. Derived from the TOKEN, never from a header. */
export function userContext(req: FastifyRequest) {
  return {
    userId: req.user?.id ?? null,
    roles: req.roles?.() ?? [],
    container: req.tenantInfo?.id ? `tenant:${req.tenantInfo.id}` : 'control'
  }
}
```

`req.userContext` was a v4 convention populated by a consumer `preHandler`; keep it if you like
the name, but derive it from `req.user` and `req.roles()` rather than from anything the caller
sends. The identity comes from the token, and so does the tenant.

### 4. Writing relations

A foreign key is a column, and a controller assigns it directly — `data.clientId = '…'`. There is
no id-to-object dance: that existed because TypeORM's active-record wanted a partial entity to
avoid an extra query. Drizzle takes the value.

```typescript
export async function update(req: FastifyRequest, reply: FastifyReply) {
  const { id } = req.parameters()
  // Only the body: an update steered by the query string is an update whose values can be put
  // in a link. `req.data()` merges the two since v5, so the distinction is now expressible.
  return orderService.on(container(req)).update(userContext(req), id, req.bodyData())
}
```

---

## 4.4 Implementation Pattern: From Controller to Service

Here is a complete example of implementing a complex endpoint (e.g., `create`) respecting the architecture.

### The Controller (`src/api/orders/controller/order.ts`)

```typescript
import { FastifyReply, FastifyRequest } from '@volcanicminds/backend'
import { orderService } from '../../../services/order.service.js'

export async function create(req: FastifyRequest, reply: FastifyReply) {
  // 1. Data Extraction
  const { id: _ignore, ...payload } = req.data()

  // 2. Rapid Logic Validation (optional if JSON Schema exists)
  if (!payload.code) {
    return reply.status(400).send(new Error('Missing order code'))
  }

  // 3. Foreign keys are columns: assign the value, there is no entity to hydrate.

  try {
    // 4. Delegate to Service, BOUND to this request's container. A service used without one
    //    throws: there is no global connection to fall back on (defects D-01, D-06).
    const result = await orderService.on(container(req)).create(userContext(req), payload)

    // 5. Response
    // If result is null or errors occur, service will have thrown exception
    return reply.code(201).send(result)
  } catch (err) {
    // Custom Error Handling
    if (err.message.includes('Access denied')) {
      return reply.status(403).send({ message: err.message })
    }
    // Rethrow for global handler (500)
    throw err
  }
}
```

### The Service (`src/services/order.service.ts`)

The service extends `BaseService` to inherit standard CRUD, but can overwrite methods or add new ones.

```typescript
// (See Part 5 for full Service Layer details)
export class OrderService extends BaseService<Order> {
  // ...
  async create(ctx: UserContext, data: any) {
    // Security Check: A Manager can create orders only for their company
    if (ctx.role === 'manager') {
      data.company = ctx.company
    }

    // Business Validation: Unique Code
    const exists = await this.repository.findOne({ where: { code: data.code } })
    if (exists) throw new Error('Order code already exists')

    // Persistence (use the context-bound repository, not global Active Record)
    const order = this.repository.create(data)
    return await this.repository.save(order)
  }
}
```

---

## 4.5 Middleware: Global vs Local

Middlewares are functions executed _before_ the handler. In `@volcanicminds/backend`, middleware configuration happens via strings in `routes.ts`.

### 1. Global Middleware (`global.*`)

If the string starts with `global.`, the framework looks for the file in two locations:

1.  `src/middleware/` (Custom application Middleware).
2.  `lib/middleware/` (Native framework Middleware, e.g., `isAuthenticated`).

**Common Native Middlewares:**

- `global.isAuthenticated`: Verifies JWT, expiration, and injects `req.user`.
- `global.isAdmin`: Verifies if user has admin role (shortcut).

### 2. Local Middleware

If the string has no prefix, the framework looks in the `middleware` folder _relative_ to the `routes.ts` file. Useful for module-specific logic.

**Mixed Configuration Example:**

```typescript
// src/api/special/routes.ts
routes: [
  {
    path: '/action',
    handler: 'special.action',
    middlewares: [
      'global.isAuthenticated', // Global: check token
      'checkBusinessHours' // Local: src/api/special/middleware/checkBusinessHours.ts
    ]
  }
]
```

---

## 4.6 JSON Schemas & Validation

Fastify uses JSON Schema to validate input and serialize output. This offers extremely high performance and automatic documentation.

### Definition (`src/schemas/*.ts`)

Every schema must have a unique `$id`.

```typescript
// src/schemas/order.ts
export const orderBodySchema = {
  $id: 'orderBodySchema',
  type: 'object',
  required: ['code', 'name'],
  properties: {
    code: { type: 'string', minLength: 3 },
    name: { type: 'string' },
    year: { type: 'number' }
  },
  additionalProperties: false // Best Practice: Refuse unknown fields
}
```

### Registration

The framework automatically loads all files in `src/schemas`.
In `routes.ts`, reference the schema using `$ref: 'ID_SCHEMA#'`.

**Note on `#`**: The `#` character at the end of `$ref` is mandatory in Fastify syntax to indicate schema root.

### Schema Overriding

If you define a schema with the same `$id` as a native framework schema (e.g., `authLoginResponseSchema`), the loader will perform a **Deep Merge**. This allows adding custom fields (e.g., `companyId` in login) without forking the library.

---

# Part 5: Service Layer Architecture

The Service Layer is where the application's "truth" resides. While Controllers handle HTTP, Services handle data.

In this stack, Services must respect three fundamental rules:

1.  **Agnostic**: They don't know `req` or `res`. They accept `UserContext` and DTOs/Objects.
2.  **Secure**: Must filter data based on user _before_ returning it (Row Level Security).
3.  **Singleton**: Instantiated once and exported for use throughout the app.

---

## 5.1 The `BaseService` Pattern

All CRUD services extend an abstract `BaseService`, so search, pagination and filtering are
written once. What changed in v5 is what a service is bound to: **a container**, not an
`EntityManager` — and where v4 let a service work without one by falling back to
`global.connection`, here there is nothing to fall back to.

### Reference implementation (`src/services/base.service.ts`)

Taken from `volcanic-backend-sample`, where it runs against a real Postgres.

```typescript
import { and, eq, inArray, isNull, type SQL, type Table } from 'drizzle-orm'
import type { DataHandle } from '@volcanicminds/backend'
import { access, executeCount, executeFind, type QueryOptions } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'
import { tablesFor, type AppTables } from '../tables/index.js'
import type { UserContext } from '../../types/index.js'

export abstract class BaseService<K extends keyof AppTables> {
  protected handle?: DataHandle

  /** Never returned, and — new in v5 — never filterable either: filtering a hash is an oracle. */
  protected sensitiveFields: string[] = []

  constructor(protected readonly tableName: K) {}

  /** Bind to the container this request works on. Returns a scoped clone. */
  on(handle?: DataHandle): this {
    const scoped = Object.create(this) as this
    scoped.handle = handle
    return scoped
  }

  protected get bound() {
    if (!this.handle) {
      throw new Error(`[${this.constructor.name}] used without a container. Call service.on(dataContext(req)).`)
    }
    const { db, dialect } = access(this.handle, this.constructor.name)
    return {
      db,
      table: tablesFor(this.handle)[this.tableName] as unknown as Table,
      options: { dialect, sensitiveFields: this.sensitiveFields } as QueryOptions
    }
  }

  /**
   * Row-level security. Whatever this returns is AND-ed AFTER everything the URL asked for,
   * `_logic` included, so no filter a caller writes reaches around it.
   */
  protected applyPermissions(_ctx: UserContext, _table: any): SQL | undefined {
    return undefined
  }

  protected alive(table: any): SQL | undefined {
    return table.deletedAt ? isNull(table.deletedAt) : undefined
  }

  async findAll(ctx: UserContext, params: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    const { db, table, options } = this.bound
    const restriction = and(...([this.alive(table), this.applyPermissions(ctx, table)].filter(Boolean) as SQL[]))
    return executeFind<any>({ db }, table, params, { ...options, extraWhere: restriction })
  }

  async count(ctx: UserContext, params: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    const { db, table, options } = this.bound
    const restriction = and(...([this.alive(table), this.applyPermissions(ctx, table)].filter(Boolean) as SQL[]))
    return executeCount({ db }, table, params, { ...options, extraWhere: restriction })
  }

  async findOne(ctx: UserContext, id: string) {
    const { db, table } = this.bound
    const t = table as any
    const where = and(...([eq(t.id, id), this.alive(t), this.applyPermissions(ctx, t)].filter(Boolean) as SQL[]))
    const rows = await db.select().from(table).where(where).limit(1)
    return rows[0] ?? null
  }

  async create(_ctx: UserContext, data: Record<string, unknown>) {
    const { db, table } = this.bound
    const rows = await db.insert(table).values(this.writable(data)).returning()
    return rows[0] ?? null
  }

  async update(ctx: UserContext, id: string, data: Record<string, unknown>) {
    const { db, table } = this.bound
    const t = table as any
    const where = and(...([eq(t.id, id), this.alive(t), this.applyPermissions(ctx, t)].filter(Boolean) as SQL[]))
    const rows = await db.update(table).set({ ...this.writable(data), updatedAt: new Date() }).where(where).returning()
    return rows[0] ?? null
  }

  /** Soft delete: the row keeps its place and stops being read. */
  async remove(ctx: UserContext, id: string) {
    const updated = await this.update(ctx, id, { deletedAt: new Date() } as Record<string, unknown>)
    return { affected: updated ? 1 : 0 }
  }

  async removeMany(ctx: UserContext, ids: string[]) {
    if (!ids.length) return 0
    const { db, table } = this.bound
    const t = table as any
    const where = and(...([inArray(t.id, ids), this.alive(t), this.applyPermissions(ctx, t)].filter(Boolean) as SQL[]))
    const rows = await db.update(table).set({ deletedAt: new Date(), updatedAt: new Date() }).where(where).returning()
    return rows.length
  }

  /**
   * The columns a caller may write, built FROM THE TABLE rather than from a denylist: a column
   * added tomorrow is writable only if it is in the table, and a key the caller invented is
   * dropped instead of reaching the database as an error nobody can read.
   */
  protected writable(data: Record<string, unknown>): Record<string, unknown> {
    const table = this.bound.table as unknown as Record<string, unknown>
    const reserved = new Set(['id', 'createdAt', 'updatedAt'])
    const out: Record<string, unknown> = {}
    for (const key of Object.keys(data)) {
      if (!reserved.has(key) && key in table) out[key] = data[key]
    }
    return out
  }
}
```

### A concrete service

```typescript
// src/services/order.service.ts
class OrderService extends BaseService<'order'> {
  constructor() {
    super('order')
  }

  protected applyPermissions(ctx: UserContext, table: any) {
    // A manager sees only their own company's orders. Returned as a condition, not applied by
    // filtering the results afterwards: filtering after the page has been cut returns short
    // pages and a wrong total.
    return ctx.roles.includes('admin') ? undefined : eq(table.companyId, ctx.companyId)
  }
}

export const orderService = new OrderService()
```

### What changed, and why it is not a rename

| v4 | v5 |
|---|---|
| `service.use(req.db)` | `service.on(dataContext(req))` |
| a service without a manager fell back to `global.connection` | a service without a handle **throws** |
| `applyPermissions` returned a `where` object merged by the query builder | it returns a `SQL` condition carried as `extraWhere`, AND-ed **last** |
| the repository came from an `EntityManager` | the table is built **for the locator** the handle addresses |
| `global.repository.X` — forbidden at runtime by a Proxy | does not exist; there is nothing to forbid |

The last row is the point. In v4 the forbidden path had to be *guarded*, because it was still
reachable; the Proxy that threw was a fence around a hole. In v5 there is no ambient container to
reach for, so the mistake is not available.

## 5.2 Security Context & RLS (Row Level Security)

`applyPermissions` is the pillar of security: instead of writing `if (role === 'admin')` in every
controller, visibility is defined once per table and enforced by the query layer.

`UserContext` is **yours** (`types/index.d.ts`) and is derived from the token — never from
anything the caller sends:

- `userId`, `roles`: from `req.user` and `req.roles()`.
- `container`: which plane this request is on, for logging and for rules that differ between them.
- whatever else your domain needs (a company, a professional id), read from the row.

### Complex example: `OrderService`

Rules: an admin sees everything; a manager sees their company's orders; a user sees orders they
worked on.

```typescript
// src/services/order.service.ts
import { and, eq, exists, sql } from 'drizzle-orm'
import { BaseService } from './base.service.js'
import type { UserContext } from '../../types/index.js'

export class OrderService extends BaseService<'order'> {
  constructor() {
    super('order')
  }

  protected applyPermissions(ctx: UserContext, table: any) {
    // 1. ADMIN: no restriction. `undefined` means "add nothing", which is not the same as
    //    "add a condition that is always true" — the query stays as short as it should be.
    if (ctx.roles.includes('admin')) return undefined

    // 2. MANAGER: their company only. A manager WITHOUT a company sees nothing, and that is
    //    written explicitly: the dangerous default here is the one that returns everything.
    if (ctx.roles.includes('manager')) {
      if (!ctx.companyId) return sql`false`
      return eq(table.companyId, ctx.companyId)
    }

    // 3. USER: their company, and only orders they worked on. EXISTS rather than a join: a join
    //    used for filtering multiplies rows and then needs a DISTINCT to undo itself.
    if (ctx.roles.includes('user')) {
      if (!ctx.professionalId || !ctx.companyId) return sql`false`
      return and(
        eq(table.companyId, ctx.companyId),
        sql`exists (
          select 1 from work_order wo
          join activity a on a.work_order_id = wo.id
          where wo.order_id = ${table.id} and a.professional_id = ${ctx.professionalId}
        )`
      )
    }

    // Default deny. An unknown role is not a role with no restrictions.
    return sql`false`
  }
}

export const orderService = new OrderService()
```

**Why the condition is returned rather than applied.** It travels as `QueryOptions.extraWhere`
and is AND-ed **after** everything the URL asked for, `_logic` included — so no expression a
client can write reaches around it. The alternative, filtering the results after the query, cuts
the page first and filters second: short pages and a wrong total.

**Default deny is written, not assumed.** Every branch that cannot establish who the caller is
returns a false condition. The failure mode of the opposite choice is not an error, it is a
response containing rows the caller should never have seen, and nothing reports it.

---

## 5.3 Relations and computed fields

There is no `addRelations` hook to override, because joins are not a property of a service. A
query that needs one writes it, and a route that allows a caller to ask for one declares it in
`allowedRelations`.

```typescript
export class ActivityService extends BaseService<'activity'> {
  /** Activities with their professional, and the hours logged against each. */
  async withHours(ctx: UserContext, params: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    const { db, table, options } = this.bound
    const { professional, timesheet } = tablesFor(this.handle!)

    // The Magic Query still parses the caller's filters; the join and the computed column are
    // this method's own business.
    const parsed = parseQuery(table, params, { ...options, extraWhere: this.applyPermissions(ctx, table) })

    return db
      .select({
        activity: table,
        professional,
        doneHours: sql<number>`coalesce((select sum(t.log_time) from timesheet t where t.activity_id = ${(table as any).id}), 0)`
      })
      .from(table)
      .leftJoin(professional, eq((table as any).professionalId, professional.id))
      .where(parsed.where)
      .orderBy(...parsed.orderBy)
      .limit(parsed.limit)
      .offset(parsed.offset)
  }
}
```

Two things worth naming:

- **The subquery is correlated and scalar**, so it costs one pass and returns one number per row.
  A `leftJoin` onto `timesheet` plus a `GROUP BY` would multiply the rows first and then collapse
  them, and every other column would have to be listed in the grouping.
- **The N+1 problem is solved by asking for the join**, not by declaring `eager: true` on a
  relation. Eager loading is a decision about one endpoint's cost written on the model, where it
  becomes a decision about every endpoint at once — which is how a list endpoint quietly becomes
  six joins.

## 5.4 Transaction Management (Complex Writes)

`BaseService` covers reads and simple writes well. When an operation spans several tables —
create an Order plus its WorkOrders plus their Activities — it has to be atomic, and the
transaction is taken **from the container**, never from a global connection.

```typescript
import { access } from '@volcanicminds/backend/db'

async createFull(ctx: UserContext, data: any) {
  const { workOrders, ...orderData } = data
  const { transaction } = access(this.handle!, 'createFull')
  const { order, workOrder } = tablesFor(this.handle!)

  // All of it or none of it. The handle's transaction is bound to THIS container, so there is
  // no way to open one against a different one by accident — which is what taking it from
  // `global.connection` allowed.
  return transaction(async (tx) => {
    const [saved] = await tx.db.insert(order).values(this.writable(orderData)).returning()

    for (const wo of workOrders) {
      await tx.db.insert(workOrder).values({ ...wo, orderId: saved.id })
    }

    return saved
  })
}
```

**No connect/commit/rollback/release by hand.** In v4 the caller opened a `QueryRunner`, started a
transaction, and was responsible for releasing it — and releasing it in the wrong place, in the
wrong order, is exactly half of defect D-01: the release ran before the reset that was supposed to
undo the session state, so the connection went back to the pool still pointing at a tenant's
schema. One owner, one release, and no session state to undo.

**A rollback that fails does not replace the error that caused it.** The first says what went
wrong; the second only says the connection is worse off.

**Engine note.** better-sqlite3 refuses an async callback outright (its driver is synchronous), so
the adapter drives `begin`/`commit`/`rollback` by statement there, while libSQL needs the driver's
